A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with HOT renamed MOT. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction scores and transport maps for language models, vision models, cross-subject fMRI, and brain-to-model alignment.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds training-trajectory alignment, broader comparisons, hierarchy measurements, and neuron-subsampling results.

M1.justification: The two-level neuron/layer transport procedure and rotation extension are retained. Section 3.4 adds a third transport optimization over checkpoint-pair costs, enabling alignment of entire training trajectories; v1 proposed this only as future work.

E1.justification: v2 adds training-trajectory alignment using two Pythia-14M runs, a distinct task on the retained STSB stimuli. Cross-subject fMRI coverage expands from V1–V4 to include lateral, dorsal, and ventral regions, confirmed by Figure 3. ImageNet and brain-to-model coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Appendices F, H, and I add global flattened OT and linear-predictivity comparators, pairwise linear predictivity for LLMs, and RSA comparisons for LLMs and fMRI. Pairwise linear predictivity for fMRI was already evaluated in v1 and is retained with expanded regional coverage.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs include 154 checkpoints per Pythia run, flattened-network comparisons, a quantitative hierarchy metric, and neuron-subsampling with refitted transport plans, including rotation-augmented LLM comparisons. The original benchmark stimulus counts and 20% held-out split descriptions are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix F tests the effect of discarding layer structure, Appendix G quantifies hierarchy previously assessed visually, and Appendix J tests sensitivity to neuron removal. Appendices H–I also expand diagnostic mapping analyses beyond v1's fMRI linear-predictivity comparison.

E5.justification: Both versions already report five random fMRI splits and mean ± standard deviation in corresponding appendix tables. v2 newly reports five-seed averaging and plotted error bars for subsampling in Appendix J, although the error-bar statistic is unspecified. It does not report increased repetition of the original experiments.

E6.justification: Cross-subject fMRI scores are replaced under expanded regional coverage: Table 2's Subject A–B HOT/MOT score changes from 0.306 to 0.244, not a same-setting performance decline. New results include checkpoint correspondences, hierarchy scores, subsampling curves, and stronger baseline scores; Table H.1 reports 0.737 for linear predictivity versus 0.558 for MOT on Llama-3.2 1B–3B. Original LLM, vision-model, and brain-to-model tables retain their values.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 formally extends the existing transport objective to checkpoints, and Appendix G defines a normalized diagonal-distance hierarchy score. These are incremental formal additions; the original transport constraints and Birkhoff–von Neumann reasoning remain unchanged. Appendix A mainly re-expresses the existing inner OT formulation.

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims demonstrated alignment across training trajectories and recovery of checkpoint correspondences missed by greedy matching. This expands the claimed capability beyond static network comparisons and converts v1's proposed future extension into a reported contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets neuron subsampling as a practical computation–accuracy tradeoff and connects alignment measurement to convergence hypotheses in the discussion. Future directions now examine factors shaping training-run alignment. Existing computational and generality limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Pythia-14M seed identities, the checkpoint sampling schedule, and the stimuli used for trajectory alignment. Appendix J documents random neuron selection and refitting. These provide reproducibility information for new experiments without a substantial expansion of implementation, hardware, or code-access information.

R1.justification: v2 adds Biderman et al. on Pythia and Cao and Yamins on the contravariance principle, and expands discussion of the already cited Platonic representation hypothesis. The principal positioning relative to soft matching and pairwise similarity methods remains unchanged.

P1.justification: HOT is renamed MOT throughout, the inner-transport explanation and discussion receive localized rewrites, and OT background moves into a new introductory appendix. Appendix organization and cross-references change, but most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, brain-alignment heatmaps expand from four to seven regions, and Figure 5 adds checkpoint transport maps. New Tables F.1–H.1 and Figures H.1–J.1 substantially expand the displays, including reorganized linear-predictivity panels, RSA maps, and an error-bar plot.

improvement.justification: Quantified hierarchy, stronger comparison methods, and repeated-seed subsampling tests make the central claims more assessable than v1's narrower comparisons and largely visual hierarchy evidence. The trajectory experiment also demonstrates a previously hypothetical extension. These benefits are tempered by unreconciled broad superiority claims: new Tables F.1 and H.1 show linear predictivity outperforming MOT on many reconstruction comparisons.
